hereditary

/huh-RED-ih-ter-ee/ · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Hereditary means passed down genetically from parent to offspring.

The breeder traced the hereditary coat pattern through six generations of her herd.

Example

A vet compiles records on 240 collies living in one valley. A particular eye defect appears in 61 of them, and every single affected dog descends from one imported sire; not one dog outside his line shows it, though all 240 share the same pastures, water, and feed. Two litters raised in different counties turn up the same defect in the same proportion. The vet concludes that the condition is hereditary.

The defect follows one sire's bloodline rather than the shared pasture, water, or feed, and reappears in pups raised elsewhere, which marks a trait travelling by descent, exactly what hereditary means.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

inherited: Inherited is the everyday word for anything received from those who came before, from a grandmother's ring to a gene for eye colour. Hereditary is the formal adjective for what descent itself transmits, and in medicine it points specifically to transmission through the parents' genes.

ancestral: Ancestral ties something to one's forebears -- ancestral land, an ancestral custom -- without saying how it travelled down. Hereditary names the mechanism: passed from parent to offspring, in medicine through the genes. A recipe can be ancestral; a blood type is hereditary.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

acquired: gained during life rather than inherited

environmental: caused by surroundings rather than by descent

Where it sits · how precisely the trait's source is identified — familial → hereditary → genetic

familial vs. hereditary: Familial says only that a trait runs in a family, which could be diet or habit as easily as descent, while hereditary says it travels in the genes.

genetic vs. hereditary: Genetic is the most precise of the three, since every hereditary trait is genetic, but a genetic change arising new in one individual is not hereditary until it is passed on.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — hered-

Root — hered-: heir (Latin heres, heredis)

Suffix — -itary

Suffix — -itary: having to do with

Put it together

Put it together: Latin heres meant an heir, the person who received an estate, and hereditas was the inheritance itself. English took the legal word and let biology borrow it, so that a gene can be inherited exactly as a farm once was. The same root passes down through heir, heritage, inherit, and heirloom.

Use the root in a new word: heirloom

Use the root in a new word: heirloom: An heirloom passes down the family line just as a hereditary trait does, and both words come from Latin heres, 'heir.'

Word Choice

technical in biology and law; neutral

Hereditary covers anything transmitted by descent, whether a gene, a title, or a monarchy. In medicine it is the narrower cousin of congenital, taught in this unit: congenital means only that a condition was present at birth, while hereditary specifies that it arrived through the parents' genes.
